RIGHT TO REPAIR ACT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Homes, Inc.

RIGHT TO REPAIR ACT — PURPOSE AND BACKGROUND DECLARATION
This information sheet describes California's Right to Repair Act (Civil Code §§ 895–945.5, enacted by Senate Bill 800 in 2002), which sets detailed construction-defect performance standards for new residential construction and establishes a mandatory prelitigation notice-and-opportunity-to-repair process a homeowner generally must follow before suing a builder for an alleged construction defect. It concerns the residence located at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield, as between Jordan Alex Lee and Acme Homes, Inc., described here as the builder of that residence. This information sheet is educational only. It does not itself constitute, serve, or complete the written notice of claim the Act requires; it does not determine that any specific condition at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield violates any standard set forth in the Act; and it does not initiate, waive, toll, extend, or complete any statutory deadline, inspection, repair offer, or legal action described in the Act. Only the notice, inspection, and repair process the Act itself describes — and, ultimately, a court or other body with authority to decide the question — can determine whether a specific condition violates the Act, or what remedy, if any, is available with respect to 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield.

WHAT THE RIGHT TO REPAIR ACT COVERS, AND HOW ITS PERFORMANCE STANDARDS ARE STRUCTURED
California's Right to Repair Act is codified at Civil Code §§ 895 through 945.5, under Title 7 of the Civil Code, titled "Requirements for Actions for Construction Defects." Its actionable-defects chapter, Civil Code § 896, states that in an action seeking recovery of damages "arising out of, or related to deficiencies in, the residential construction, design, specifications, surveying, planning, supervision, testing, or observation of construction," a builder — and, to the extent set out in the Act's prelitigation chapter (Chapter 4, commencing with § 910), a general contractor, subcontractor, material supplier, individual product manufacturer, or design professional — is liable for, and the claimant's claims are generally limited to, violation of the specific standards § 896 lists. Section 896 further states that "[t]his title applies to original construction intended to be sold as an individual dwelling unit," and separately that "[a]s to condominium conversions, this title does not apply to or does not supersede any other statutory or common law." Rather than relying on a general negligence or implied-warranty standard, § 896 sets out a long, itemized list of specific performance standards organized by subject matter: subdivision (a) addresses water issues (for example, doors, windows, roofs, decks, and foundations), (b) structural issues, (c) soil issues, (d) fire protection issues, (e) plumbing and sewer issues, (f) electrical system issues, and (g) a further set of standards addressing other areas of construction, including exterior pathways, paint and stains, dryer ducts, and landscaping.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "In any action seeking recovery of damages arising out of, or related to deficiencies in, the residential construction, design, specifications, surveying, planning, supervision, testing, or observation of construction, a builder, and to the extent set forth in Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 910), a general contractor, subcontractor, material supplier, individual product manufacturer, or design professional, shall, except as specifically set forth in this title, be liable for, and the claimant's claims or causes of action shall be limited to violation of, the following standards, except as specifically set forth in this title."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 896 (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code § 896, introductory paragraph (liability for violation of the listed standards) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=896.)
  "This title applies to original construction intended to be sold as an individual dwelling unit. As to condominium conversions, this title does not apply to or does not supersede any other statutory or common law."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 896 (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code § 896, introductory paragraph (applicability to original construction; condominium-conversion carve-out) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=896.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's actual construction-defect performance-standards scheme for new residential construction — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular project, and not a claim that other states have a comparable statutory scheme (most do not). Both citations below are drawn from the same statutory section, Civil Code § 896 (its unnumbered introductory paragraph), rather than from independently authored sources, so they corroborate one internally consistent provision rather than two separate ones. This clause does not attempt to reproduce § 896's very long, detailed list of specific numbered performance standards; a companion clause quotes a small, genuinely verified sample of them rather than summarizing the list exhaustively. This clause also does not state whether a particular structure is "original construction intended to be sold as an individual dwelling unit" as the statute uses that phrase, whether a particular transaction is a "condominium conversion," or whether the Act — as opposed to ordinary negligence, contract, or warranty law — governs a particular claim.

EXAMPLES OF § 896'S ACTIONABLE PERFORMANCE STANDARDS, INCLUDING THEIR EMBEDDED TIME LIMITS
Civil Code § 896's list of actionable standards is extensive — it covers dozens of specific defect categories across water intrusion, structural, soil, fire protection, plumbing, electrical, and other systems — and this clause does not attempt to summarize it exhaustively. Instead, a few individually verified examples illustrate both the specificity of the standards and a feature that runs through several of them: some standards carry their own embedded time limit, stated within the same numbered standard, on when an action may be brought for a violation of that particular standard. A structural example, from subdivision (b)(1), carries no such stated limit in its own text: "Foundations, load bearing components, and slabs, shall not contain significant cracks or significant vertical displacement." By contrast, the plumbing-and-sewer standard in subdivision (e) states both the performance requirement and its own four-year limit: "Plumbing and sewer systems shall be installed to operate properly and shall not materially impair the use of the structure by its inhabitants. However, no action may be brought for a violation of this subdivision more than four years after close of escrow." The electrical-system standard in subdivision (f) uses parallel four-year language. Other standards in subdivision (g) carry shorter embedded limits: the interunit noise-transmission standard in (g)(6) states that "no action shall be brought pursuant to this paragraph more than one year from the original occupancy of the adjacent unit," while the paint-and-stains standard in (g)(10) states a five-year limit running from close of escrow. These standard-specific time limits operate alongside, and independently of, the Act's outer 10-year limitations period discussed in a separate clause of this document.

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 896(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code § 896(b)(1), structural standard for foundations, load-bearing components, and slabs (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=896.)
  "Plumbing and sewer systems shall be installed to operate properly and shall not materially impair the use of the structure by its inhabitants. However, no action may be brought for a violation of this subdivision more than four years after close of escrow."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 896(e) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code § 896(e), plumbing and sewer standard, with its embedded four-year limit (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=896.)
  "However, no action shall be brought pursuant to this paragraph more than one year from the original occupancy of the adjacent unit."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 896(g)(6) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code § 896(g)(6), interunit noise-transmission standard, with its embedded one-year limit (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=896.)
  "Paint and stains shall be applied in such a manner so as not to cause deterioration of the building surfaces for the length of time specified by the paint or stain manufacturers' representations, if any. However, no action shall be brought pursuant to this paragraph more than five years from close of escrow."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 896(g)(10) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code § 896(g)(10), paint-and-stains standard, with its embedded five-year limit (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=896.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of specific, verified examples drawn from California's actionable construction-defect standards — not a claim that these four examples represent the full scope, severity, or relative importance of § 896's standards, and not a claim about which state's law governs a particular defect. All four citations below are numbered standards within the same statutory section, Civil Code § 896, rather than independently authored sources, so they corroborate one internally consistent list rather than four separate ones. This clause deliberately does not attempt to reproduce § 896's full list of standards (which runs to dozens of numbered items across subdivisions (a) through (g)), and it does not state whether a particular observed condition meets the technical elements of any specific standard, when a particular standard's clock (such as "close of escrow" or "original occupancy") actually started running on particular facts, or what standard (if any) applies to a defect not resembling these four examples.

THE MANDATORY PRELITIGATION NOTICE OF CLAIM
Before filing an action against any party alleged to have contributed to a violation of the § 896 standards, Civil Code § 910 requires a claimant to initiate a prelitigation procedure, beginning with written notice. Section 910(a) requires the claimant or the claimant's legal representative to "provide written notice via certified mail, overnight mail, or personal delivery to the builder" of the claimant's claim that the residence's construction violates one or more of the § 896 standards, and specifies what the notice must contain: it "shall provide the claimant's name, address, and preferred method of contact, and shall state that the claimant alleges a violation pursuant to this part against the builder, and shall describe the claim in reasonable detail sufficient to determine the nature and location, to the extent known, of the claimed violation." For a group of homeowners or an association, the notice may identify claimants solely by address or another description sufficient to apprise the builder of the affected residences. The statute treats this written notice as formally significant — "[t]hat document shall have the same force and effect as a notice of commencement of a legal proceeding" — and it is distinct from, and not satisfied by, a request made instead through a builder's own contractual, warranty, or customer-service process. Once notice is served, Civil Code § 913 requires the builder or the builder's representative to "acknowledge, in writing, receipt of the notice of the claim within 14 days after receipt of the notice of the claim," and, if the claimant is represented by an attorney, to include that attorney in subsequent substantive communications.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The claimant or his or her legal representative shall provide written notice via certified mail, overnight mail, or personal delivery to the builder, in the manner prescribed in this section, of the claimant's claim that the construction of his or her residence violates any of the standards set forth in Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 896). That notice shall provide the claimant's name, address, and preferred method of contact, and shall state that the claimant alleges a violation pursuant to this part against the builder, and shall describe the claim in reasonable detail sufficient to determine the nature and location, to the extent known, of the claimed violation. ... That document shall have the same force and effect as a notice of commencement of a legal proceeding."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 910(a) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code § 910(a), required contents and effect of the written notice of claim (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=910.)
  "A builder or his or her representative shall acknowledge, in writing, receipt of the notice of the claim within 14 days after receipt of the notice of the claim."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 913 (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code § 913, builder's 14-day deadline to acknowledge the notice of claim (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=913.)

The two citations below are to different code sections (§ 910 and § 913) within the same statutory chapter (Chapter 4 of Title 7, added by the same 2002 enacting bill, SB 800), rather than to independently authored sources outside that single legislative scheme; they are treated here as corroborating one internally consistent prelitigation process rather than as independent confirmations from unrelated sources. This clause does not state what level of factual detail satisfies "reasonable detail sufficient to determine the nature and location" of a claimed violation on particular facts, whether a particular notice was properly served under § 910's specified delivery methods, or what happens under this title when the underlying claim is not the kind the Act's prelitigation chapter reaches at all (for example, claims outside § 896's scope).

THE BUILDER'S INSPECTION AND REPAIR-OFFER PROCESS, AND THE HOMEOWNER'S RESPONSE
If a builder elects to inspect the claimed unmet standards, Civil Code § 916(a) requires the builder to "complete the initial inspection and testing within 14 days after acknowledgment of receipt of the notice of the claim, at a mutually convenient date and time," with all inspection and testing costs borne by the builder. Within 30 days of that inspection (or a second inspection, if the builder reasonably requests one), Civil Code § 917 allows the builder to "offer in writing to repair the violation," and requires that offer to compensate the homeowner for applicable damages recoverable under § 944, and to include "a detailed, specific, step-by-step statement identifying the particular violation that is being repaired, explaining the nature, scope, and location of the repair, and setting a reasonable completion date for the repair," along with the names, license numbers, and contact information of the contractors the builder intends to use. Once the homeowner receives that offer, Civil Code § 918 gives the homeowner 30 days to authorize the builder to proceed, or, at the homeowner's option, to instead request "the names, addresses, telephone numbers, and license numbers for up to three alternative contractors who are not owned or financially controlled by the builder and who regularly conduct business in the county where the structure is located" — after which the statute sets further deadlines (a 20-day additional inspection window if the homeowner so elects, 35 days for the builder to present a choice of contractors, and 20 more days for the homeowner to authorize a repair).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 916(a) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code § 916(a), builder's 14-day deadline to complete the initial inspection and testing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=916.)
  "Within 30 days of the initial or, if requested, second inspection or testing, the builder may offer in writing to repair the violation. ... Any such offer shall be accompanied by a detailed, specific, step-by-step statement identifying the particular violation that is being repaired, explaining the nature, scope, and location of the repair, and setting a reasonable completion date for the repair."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 917 (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code § 917, the builder's written offer to repair and its required contents (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=917.)
  "Upon receipt of the offer to repair, the homeowner shall have 30 days to authorize the builder to proceed with the repair. The homeowner may alternatively request, at the homeowner's sole option and discretion, that the builder provide the names, addresses, telephone numbers, and license numbers for up to three alternative contractors who are not owned or financially controlled by the builder and who regularly conduct business in the county where the structure is located."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 918 (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code § 918, homeowner's 30-day response window and right to request alternative contractors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=918.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's actual builder-inspection and repair-offer timeline under the Right to Repair Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular claim, and not a claim that other states impose a comparable process. The three citations below (§§ 916, 917, and 918) are separate code sections within the same statutory chapter (Chapter 4 of Title 7, added by the same 2002 enacting bill, SB 800) rather than independently authored sources outside that single legislative scheme, and are treated here as corroborating one internally consistent process rather than as independent confirmations. This clause does not reproduce every procedural detail of §§ 916 through 918 (for example, the second-inspection process under § 916(c), or the consequences under § 916(d) if a builder fails to inspect at all, which a separate clause of this document does not independently verify), and it does not state what happens on particular facts if a deadline described here is missed, disputed, or extended by agreement.

THE ACT'S OUTER LIMITATIONS PERIOD, AND TOLLING DURING THE PRELITIGATION PROCESS
Apart from the shorter, standard-specific time limits embedded within particular § 896 standards, the Right to Repair Act sets a general outer boundary on when an action may be brought at all. Civil Code § 941(a) provides: "Except as specifically set forth in this title, no action may be brought to recover under this title more than 10 years after substantial completion of the improvement but not later than the date of recordation of a valid notice of completion." Separately, Civil Code § 927 addresses what happens to an otherwise-running limitations period while the prelitigation notice-and-repair process is underway: "If the applicable statute of limitations has otherwise run during this process, the time period for filing a complaint or other legal remedies for violation of any provision of this title, or for a claim of inadequate repair, is extended from the time of the original claim by the claimant to 100 days after the repair is completed, whether or not the particular violation is the one being repaired." Section 927 also addresses the builder's non-participation: if the builder fails to timely acknowledge the claim, elects not to proceed under the statutory process, or fails to timely request an inspection, the filing period is instead extended "to 45 days after the time for responding to the notice of claim has expired."

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 941(a) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code § 941(a), 10-year outer limitations period (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=941.)

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 927 (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code § 927, tolling of the filing period during and after the prelitigation process (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=927.)

The two citations below (§ 941(a) and § 927) are separate code sections within the same statutory title (Title 7, added by the same 2002 enacting bill, SB 800) rather than independently authored sources outside that single legislative scheme. This clause does not state how the 10-year period under § 941(a) interacts, on particular facts, with the shorter standard-specific periods embedded in individual § 896 standards described in a companion clause, does not address § 941's separate rules on tolling doctrine generally or on indemnity actions, and does not state when a particular improvement reached "substantial completion" or when a particular "notice of completion" was validly recorded.

RECOVERABLE DAMAGES AND THE ACT'S STATUTORY AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSES
Civil Code § 944 limits what a homeowner may recover in a damages claim under the Right to Repair Act: "the homeowner is only entitled to damages for the reasonable value of repairing any violation of the standards set forth in this title, the reasonable cost of repairing any damages caused by the repair efforts, the reasonable cost of repairing and rectifying any damages resulting from the failure of the home to meet the standards, the reasonable cost of removing and replacing any improper repair by the builder, reasonable relocation and storage expenses, lost business income if the home was used as a principal place of a business licensed to be operated from the home, reasonable investigative costs for each established violation, and all other costs or fees recoverable by contract or statute." Separately, Civil Code § 945.5 gives a builder (and, correspondingly, a general contractor, subcontractor, material supplier, individual product manufacturer, or design professional) a defined set of affirmative defenses, available "under the principles of comparative fault," that can excuse liability in whole or in part — including, among others, an "unforeseen act of nature" exceeding the applicable design criteria (§ 945.5(a)), a homeowner's "unreasonable failure to minimize or prevent" damages, including failing to allow reasonable and timely access for inspection and repair or failing to give timely notice after discovering a violation (§ 945.5(b)), and a homeowner's failure to follow the builder's or manufacturer's written maintenance recommendations, where the builder shows those recommendations were reasonably communicated and reasonable when issued (§ 945.5(c)).

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 944 (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code § 944, damages recoverable under the Act (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=944.)
  "A builder, general contractor, subcontractor, material supplier, individual product manufacturer, or design professional, under the principles of comparative fault pertaining to affirmative defenses, may be excused, in whole or in part, from any obligation, damage, loss, or liability if the builder, general contractor, subcontractor, material supplier, individual product manufacturer, or design professional, can demonstrate any of the following affirmative defenses in response to a claimed violation: (a) To the extent it is caused by an unforeseen act of nature which caused the structure not to meet the standard."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 945.5(a)-(c) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code § 945.5, statutory affirmative defenses (unforeseen act of nature; homeowner's failure to mitigate; failure to follow maintenance recommendations) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=945.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's actual damages measure and statutory affirmative defenses under the Right to Repair Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular claim's damages or defenses, and not a claim that other states provide a comparable statutory defense list. The two citations below (§ 944 and § 945.5) are separate code sections within the same statutory chapter (Chapter 5 of Title 7, added or amended by the same 2002/2003 enacting legislation) rather than independently authored sources outside that single legislative scheme. This clause does not reproduce all of § 945.5's defenses (it also lists, among others, a homeowner's alterations or misuse, a builder's successful repair of the particular violation, and the running of the applicable time limitation, in § 945.5(d) through (g), not independently quoted here), and it does not state whether a particular defense would actually succeed, in whole or in part, on any specific set of facts — that determination belongs to a court or other body with authority to decide the question.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT — RIGHT TO REPAIR ACT INFORMATION SHEET ONLY
I have reviewed this information sheet describing California's Right to Repair Act (Civil Code §§ 895–945.5), including its construction-defect performance standards and its mandatory prelitigation notice-and-opportunity-to-repair process, in connection with the residence located at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield and the builder identified here as Acme Homes, Inc. I understand that this document is informational only: it does not itself constitute, serve, or complete a written notice of claim under Civil Code § 910; it does not determine that any specific condition at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield violates any standard set forth in the Act; and it does not initiate, waive, toll, extend, or complete any statutory deadline, inspection, repair offer, or legal action described in the Act.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________

It does not constitute legal advice about any specific defect, notice, deadline, or claim, and it does not appoint anyone, waive any right, or take any action with respect to any actual claim against Acme Homes, Inc. or any other party.]

expectedJSON.body: Before filing an action against any party alleged to have contributed to a violation of the § 896 standards, Civil Code § 910 requires a claimant to initiate a prelitigation procedure, beginning with written notice. Section 910(a) requires the claimant or the claimant's legal representative to "provide written notice via certified mail, overnight mail, or personal delivery to the builder" of the claimant's claim that the residence's construction violates one or more of the § 896 standards, and specifies what the notice must contain: it "shall provide the claimant's name, address, and preferred method of contact, and shall state that the claimant alleges a violation pursuant to this part against the builder, and shall describe the claim in reasonable detail sufficient to determine the nature and location, to the extent known, of the claimed violation." For a group of homeowners or an association, the notice may identify claimants solely by address or another description sufficient to apprise the builder of the affected residences. The statute treats this written notice as formally significant — "[t]hat document shall have the same force and effect as a notice of commencement of a legal proceeding" — and it is distinct from, and not satisfied by, a request made instead through a builder's own contractual, warranty, or customer-service process. Once notice is served, Civil Code § 913 requires the builder or the builder's representative to "acknowledge, in writing, receipt of the notice of the claim within 14 days after receipt of the notice of the claim," and, if the claimant is represented by an attorney, to include that attorney in subsequent substantive communications.

citations.quote: The claimant or his or her legal representative shall provide written notice via certified mail, overnight mail, or personal delivery to the builder, in the manner prescribed in this section, of the claimant's claim that the construction of his or her residence violates any of the standards set forth in Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 896). That notice shall provide the claimant's name, address, and preferred method of contact, and shall state that the claimant alleges a violation pursuant to this part against the builder, and shall describe the claim in reasonable detail sufficient to determine the nature and location, to the extent known, of the claimed violation. ... That document shall have the same force and effect as a notice of commencement of a legal proceeding.

expectedJSON.body: If a builder elects to inspect the claimed unmet standards, Civil Code § 916(a) requires the builder to "complete the initial inspection and testing within 14 days after acknowledgment of receipt of the notice of the claim, at a mutually convenient date and time," with all inspection and testing costs borne by the builder. Within 30 days of that inspection (or a second inspection, if the builder reasonably requests one), Civil Code § 917 allows the builder to "offer in writing to repair the violation," and requires that offer to compensate the homeowner for applicable damages recoverable under § 944, and to include "a detailed, specific, step-by-step statement identifying the particular violation that is being repaired, explaining the nature, scope, and location of the repair, and setting a reasonable completion date for the repair," along with the names, license numbers, and contact information of the contractors the builder intends to use. Once the homeowner receives that offer, Civil Code § 918 gives the homeowner 30 days to authorize the builder to proceed, or, at the homeowner's option, to instead request "the names, addresses, telephone numbers, and license numbers for up to three alternative contractors who are not owned or financially controlled by the builder and who regularly conduct business in the county where the structure is located" — after which the statute sets further deadlines (a 20-day additional inspection window if the homeowner so elects, 35 days for the builder to present a choice of contractors, and 20 more days for the homeowner to authorize a repair).

expectedJSON.body: Apart from the shorter, standard-specific time limits embedded within particular § 896 standards, the Right to Repair Act sets a general outer boundary on when an action may be brought at all. Civil Code § 941(a) provides: "Except as specifically set forth in this title, no action may be brought to recover under this title more than 10 years after substantial completion of the improvement but not later than the date of recordation of a valid notice of completion." Separately, Civil Code § 927 addresses what happens to an otherwise-running limitations period while the prelitigation notice-and-repair process is underway: "If the applicable statute of limitations has otherwise run during this process, the time period for filing a complaint or other legal remedies for violation of any provision of this title, or for a claim of inadequate repair, is extended from the time of the original claim by the claimant to 100 days after the repair is completed, whether or not the particular violation is the one being repaired." Section 927 also addresses the builder's non-participation: if the builder fails to timely acknowledge the claim, elects not to proceed under the statutory process, or fails to timely request an inspection, the filing period is instead extended "to 45 days after the time for responding to the notice of claim has expired."

expectedJSON.body: Civil Code § 944 limits what a homeowner may recover in a damages claim under the Right to Repair Act: "the homeowner is only entitled to damages for the reasonable value of repairing any violation of the standards set forth in this title, the reasonable cost of repairing any damages caused by the repair efforts, the reasonable cost of repairing and rectifying any damages resulting from the failure of the home to meet the standards, the reasonable cost of removing and replacing any improper repair by the builder, reasonable relocation and storage expenses, lost business income if the home was used as a principal place of a business licensed to be operated from the home, reasonable investigative costs for each established violation, and all other costs or fees recoverable by contract or statute." Separately, Civil Code § 945.5 gives a builder (and, correspondingly, a general contractor, subcontractor, material supplier, individual product manufacturer, or design professional) a defined set of affirmative defenses, available "under the principles of comparative fault," that can excuse liability in whole or in part — including, among others, an "unforeseen act of nature" exceeding the applicable design criteria (§ 945.5(a)), a homeowner's "unreasonable failure to minimize or prevent" damages, including failing to allow reasonable and timely access for inspection and repair or failing to give timely notice after discovering a violation (§ 945.5(b)), and a homeowner's failure to follow the builder's or manufacturer's written maintenance recommendations, where the builder shows those recommendations were reasonably communicated and reasonable when issued (§ 945.5(c)).
